case_study_insert.main_stem: Bellwether Dairy (BWD) is a dairy processing partnership in the food industry rather than a sole trader, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Aoife Bellwether, the business supplies supermarket chains with locally sourced cheese and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. BWD plans to invest $330,000 in a new automated cheese packing line to cut waste, financed by a $210,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $156,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.00, and produces 65,000 units a year. BWD faces two problems: absenteeism is high among packing staff and milk waste has reached 4.7% of input.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report - Q3 2025: BWD packed 15,600 units of cheese last quarter at a defect rate of 1.9%, down from 3.2% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 18 a month. Milk waste reached 4.7% of input. Delivery lead time averages 2.6 days. A survey of 380 supermarket buyers found 57% would pay up to $0.35 more for locally sourced dairy, and 44% check farm-origin labels. A skills audit shows 11 of 28 staff have not been trained on the new packing seals; the local college charges $620 per place.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing debt-service costs on BWD's $210,000 loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 an hour from April 2026. (3) Feed and dairy input costs have risen 10.2% year-on-year, food inflation is 6.8% and consumer spending on locally sourced cheese grew 3.7%.

questions.question_text: BWD is a partnership funding a $330,000 expansion with a $210,000 bank loan and $120,000 retained profit. Explain two benefits for BWD of operating as a partnership rather than a sole trader.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A partnership allows Aoife Bellwether to share the $330,000 investment risk and the management workload with other partners, rather than carrying all of the $210,000 loan liability alone as a sole trader would. With a workforce of 28 and 4.7% milk waste to control, shared decision-making under laissez-faire leadership brings different skills to quality and packing problems, improving the $9.00 product without overburdening one owner.

Point 2: Partners can contribute extra capital and creditworthiness, making the $210,000 bank loan easier to secure than for a single owner, and profits can be retained as $120,000 for the new cheese packing line. Unlike a sole trader, the business survives if one partner leaves, which reassures supermarket chains about continuity of locally sourced supply. Shares of profit are agreed in advance in the partnership deed, reducing disputes while the 65,000-unit output is maintained, and the shared management load lets Aoife Bellwether focus on the 4.7% milk waste problem rather than handling every decision alone.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: BWD is promoting a new locally sourced cheese range. Consider farmers' market tastings, local radio advertising, or local newspaper coupons. Which should BWD choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Farmers' market tastings: Tastings let shoppers try the cheese and speak to Aoife Bellwether about the farm origin, directly using the 57% of 380 buyers who would pay $0.35 more for locally sourced dairy and the 44% who check farm-origin labels. It builds loyalty and gives immediate feedback on quality. The limit is scale: a market reaches only local visitors, and with a workforce of 28 and high absenteeism, staffing several events could strain the 15,600-unit packing schedule.

Local radio advertising: Radio is relatively cheap and can reach the whole regional catchment quickly, repeating the local-source message to drivers and shoppers. It suits a perishable product with a 2.6-day delivery lead time. Its weakness is that adverts cannot show or taste the cheese, and the message is easily forgotten; 44% of buyers check labels in store, so radio alone may not convert to purchases of the $9.00 product.

Local newspaper coupons: Coupons give a measurable, price-led reason to try the range and can be clipped by exactly the shoppers already buying supermarket cheese. They are low cost per unit and traceable. However, discounting undercuts the $0.35 premium that 57% of buyers will pay and can train customers to wait for offers, squeezing the $3.80 contribution per unit needed to justify the $330,000 line.

Recommendation: BWD should choose farmers' market tastings. They convert the 57% premium preference into trial and prove origin to the 44% who check labels, without discounting. Radio is rejected because it cannot demonstrate quality and is forgettable; coupons are rejected because they erode the premium and the contribution funding the $210,000 loan. BWD can support tastings with cheap social posts later.

questions.question_text: BWD's absenteeism is high and milk waste has reached 4.7%. Explain two benefits for BWD of offering a productivity bonus to its packing staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A productivity bonus gives the 28 staff a direct financial incentive to attend and to pack accurately, which can reduce the absenteeism that disrupts the 15,600 units packed last quarter and help cut the 1.9% defect rate. Under laissez-faire leadership, a bonus sets a clear target without heavy supervision, so workers have a reason to protect the $9.00 product and reduce the 4.7% milk waste.

Point 2: Linking pay to output and quality encourages staff to suggest better sealing routines on the new $330,000 packing line, protecting the $3.80 contribution per unit and the 65,000-unit target. Because the bonus is paid only when productivity rises, BWD avoids a fixed rise in the wage bill, which matters while a $210,000 loan is being repaid and feed costs rise 10.2%. It also helps retain skilled staff, cutting the $620 per place training cost for the 11 of 28 still untrained.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: BWD wants to raise commitment among its packing staff. Consider job enrichment or team working. Which should BWD choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Job enrichment: Giving workers fuller responsibility for a whole packing batch, including checking the new seals, makes the work more meaningful and uses the 11 of 28 staff still needing training as a chance to build skill. It suits a flat partnership and can reduce the 1.9% defect rate and 4.7% milk waste because staff own the result. The risk is that under laissez-faire leadership some workers may feel unsupported when given more responsibility, and enrichment can be slow to show results where absenteeism is high.

Team working: Organising the 28 staff into small teams that rotate through packing and quality checks spreads knowledge, cuts repetitive work and lets experienced members train others without paying every $620 college place. Teams can spot waste faster, protecting the 15,600 units and the $9.00 selling price. Teams also spread knowledge so that no single absence stops the packing line, which matters given the high absenteeism reported, and they help protect the 2.6-day delivery lead time to supermarket chains. The limitation is that teams need clear goals; without them, group norms may allow absence to continue, and high absenteeism can still leave a team short-handed.

Decision: BWD should choose team working. It directly uses existing staff to spread skills and reduce the 4.7% waste without extra training fees, and it fits a workforce of 28 already organised flat. Job enrichment is rejected because, under laissez-faire leadership, added responsibility without support could raise stress and absenteeism rather than cut it; BWD can add enrichment later once teams are stable and the $330,000 line is running smoothly.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BWD's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $156,000 / ($9.00 - $3.80) = $156,000 / $5.20 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.00 - $3.80 = $5.20. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.20.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BWD's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with 65,000 units actual output, giving a margin of safety of 35,000 units, to judge whether to run the new cheese packing line at capacity.
2. Use $5.20 contribution to test the $0.35 premium: if won, contribution becomes $5.55 ($5.20 + $0.35), showing the cushion against the 10.2% feed cost rise.
3. Combine $156,000 fixed costs and $5.20 contribution to set the volume needed to service the $210,000 bank loan before committing more capital to the $330,000 line.
4. Unit cost of $6.20 ($156,000 / 65,000 + $3.80) can be benchmarked to detect the 4.7% milk waste and the 1.9% defect rate, protecting the $9.00 price.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.20 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 35,000-unit margin of safety; testing the $0.35 premium; loan-service volume targets; unit-cost benchmarking at $6.20.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BWD's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BWD's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.24 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.72 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $88,000 inventories + $72,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $200,000; 2025 current assets = $96,000 + $104,000 + $30,000 = $230,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $160,000 was $200,000 / $160,000 = 1.25; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $185,000 was $230,000 / $185,000 = 1.24. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $200,000 - $88,000 = $112,000 in 2024, giving $112,000 / $160,000 = 0.70, and $230,000 - $96,000 = $134,000 in 2025, giving $134,000 / $185,000 = 0.72.

Evaluation: Liquidity is broadly flat but the mix has weakened. Cover edged down from 1.25 to 1.24 because current liabilities rose from $160,000 to $185,000 almost as fast as current assets grew from $200,000 to $230,000. The liquid-asset measure rose slightly from 0.70 to 0.72, which looks better, but this was achieved while cash fell from $40,000 to $30,000 and inventories rose from $88,000 to $96,000. Trade receivables jumped from $72,000 to $104,000, tying up cash with supermarket chains; if those customers pay late, the small improvement in liquid cover could quickly unwind. Servicing the $210,000 loan while funding a $330,000 packing line leaves little spare cash, and the 4.7% milk waste adds pressure.

Conclusion: BWD's liquidity has not clearly improved. Overall cover slipped and the modest rise in the liquid-asset measure is offset by lower cash and much higher receivables, so the position is more dependent on collection. Tighter credit control is needed before further borrowing.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BWD of introducing quality control inspection for its cheese packing.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Inspecting finished packs can catch seal failures before they reach supermarket chains, directly cutting the 1.9% defect rate and the customer complaints that have already fallen from 33 to 18 a month. Better quality protects the 57% of 380 buyers willing to pay $0.35 more for locally sourced dairy and supports the $9.00 selling price, which is vital while the $330,000 packing line must prove itself and feed costs rise 10.2%.

Disadvantage: Inspection adds staff time and cost to a workforce of 28 where absenteeism is high, and it detects faults only after waste has occurred, so it does not reduce the 4.7% milk waste at source. Under laissez-faire leadership, inconsistent inspection standards may creep in, and rejecting batches late could delay the 2.6-day delivery lead time to supermarkets. With $3.80 variable cost per unit and $156,000 fixed costs, the extra quality cost would squeeze contribution unless the $0.35 premium is fully accepted.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in feed and dairy input costs will affect BWD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If BWD's $210,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $210,000 = $1,575, which is small against fixed costs of $156,000 and a $330,000 expansion. If the loan is fixed-rate there is no immediate effect. Higher rates may make supermarket chains cautious and raise future borrowing costs, but the direct annual hit is modest and can be capped by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.41): BWD has a workforce of 28, yet the insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The honest measure is productivity: 65,000 units / 28 staff = about 2,321 units per worker. If that holds, the rise can be absorbed within the $3.80 variable cost and $5.20 contribution; if high absenteeism lowers output, unit labour cost rises. It is permanent but cannot be quantified from the insert.

Input cost inflation (10.2% feed and dairy): The insert does not decompose the $3.80 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is defensible: if all of the $3.80 rose 10.2%, that is 10.2% x $3.80 = about $0.39 per unit, or roughly $25,000 a year at 65,000 units. That directly reduces the $5.20 contribution servicing the $210,000 loan. BWD can recover part through the $0.35 premium accepted by 57% of buyers, and locally sourced branding helps protect the $9.00 price.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in feed and dairy input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 65,000 units and erodes contribution repeatedly, far above the $1,575 interest effect; the wage rise is serious but unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity, while input inflation directly attacks the margin that funds the new packing line.
